outline.description: Sets out who the parties are, what records were sought, how the FBI processed the request, and how the dispute unfolded in the district court leading to this appeal.
subtopics: Farahi’s immigration history and DHS’s reliance on FBI evidence in removal proceedings
FOIA request scope: approximately 10,750 pages and 80 CDs located
Initial disclosures and withholdings; FBI’s 2019 summary-judgment motion
Public and ex parte Hardy declarations; district court’s 2022 order seeking updates due to staleness and segregability concerns
Renewed motion with public and ex parte Bender declarations; district court’s grant of summary judgment
Appeal to the D.C. Circuit

outline.chapter_title: FOIA Framework, Exemption 7(A), and Standards of Review
outline.description: Explains the statutory requirements relevant to this case and the standards guiding judicial review.
subtopics: FOIA’s disclosure mandate and burden on the government to justify exemptions (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(B))
Exemption 7(A): threshold “compiled for law enforcement purposes” and the “could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings” requirement
CREW and Juarez: proceedings must be pending or reasonably anticipated; ongoing criminal investigations qualify
Agency deference: FBI’s law-enforcement expertise and heightened deference in national security/counterterrorism contexts (Campbell; CNSS)
Segregability duty: reasonably segregable nonexempt portions must be released (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(ii), (b)) and reliance on detailed affidavits (Mead; Juarez)
Category-by-category withholdings standard (Gallant; CREW)
De novo review of summary judgment in FOIA cases

outline.description: Analyzes how the court determined that the records were compiled for law enforcement purposes and the evidentiary showings supporting that finding.
subtopics: Rational nexus requirement: link to agency law-enforcement duties and to a possible security risk or federal law violation (Pratt; Campbell)
Public Hardy declaration: investigations into national security and international terrorism; association with individuals involved in such violations
Ex parte Hardy declaration: added specificity on investigation’s nature and scope

Context from immigration proceedings: Farahi’s alleged ties to designated terrorist organizations and individuals (e.g., Muslim Brotherhood, KSM, Padilla; Holy Land Foundation; Global Relief Foundation)
Holding: FBI met the 7 threshold given its role and the record

outline.chapter_title: Interference with Pending or Anticipated Proceedings under Exemption 7(A)
outline.description: Details the court’s reasoning that disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with ongoing or reasonably anticipated enforcement proceedings, and addresses the ‘staleness’ concern.
subtopics: Interference rationale: disclosure would tip off targets to scope and direction of investigation (a recognized 7(A) justification)
Evidence of pendency: Hardy’s public attestation of ongoing proceedings plus ex parte elaboration
Bender’s declarations as updates confirming continued pendency as of March 2023
Addressing CREW’s caution about vagueness: Bender’s brevity read in context of detailed Hardy showings and prior district court finding that the FBI had ‘seemingly’ met its burden
Role of national-security deference and breadth of the counterterrorism investigation in finding ongoing proceedings plausible
Conclusion: existence of a concrete prospective law-enforcement proceeding established; Exemption 7(A) satisfied

outline.chapter_title: Segregability, Categorical Withholdings, and Use of Ex Parte Declarations
outline.description: Explains the court’s treatment of segregability, challenges to categorical descriptions, and the propriety of ex parte submissions in FOIA litigation.
subtopics: Segregability standard: reasonably segregable portions must be released; when nonexempt material is inextricably intertwined or line-by-line interspersed, withholding in full may be proper (Mead; Juarez; Perioperative Services)
District court’s reliance on Bender’s supplemental ex parte declaration to find no meaningful segregable information
Farahi’s volume-based argument rejected: FOIA protects information, not isolated words; quantity does not imply meaningful segregability
Challenge to categorical withholdings forfeited due to lack of specific argument showing categories were overbroad (Gallant; CREW; Khine)
Propriety of ex parte submissions: plaintiff did not object below; necessity in national-security FOIA cases to avoid revealing the very information at issue (Perioperative Services)
Disposition: affirmance of summary judgment for the FBI
